sources.title: Monthly maintenance records
caveats: Fictional exercise data. Selected records are not full-fleet totals.
Monthly maintenance for eight buses
Fictional exercise records for eight selected buses, not all 172 fleet vehicles. Complete months: October 2024–September 2026. Zero
means none recorded in the monthly ledger. Vehicle ID and month identify the same record across the cost, maintenance and usage
views. Repair jobs are not roadside breakdowns. Unavailable hours measure vehicle holds, not passenger delay. Required routine
service and additional component work are separate categories.
Monthly maintenance records

October detailed records remain separate. Full definitions are in the monthly-history CSV handout.

caveats: Fictional exercise data. Selected records are not full-fleet totals.
Selected component observations
Twelve selected visits during the monthly-history period. This is not the full repair or inspection ledger. Costs and holds are
already included in monthly totals. Blank measurements mean not applicable or not supplied. Component attention differs from
required routine servicing.
Dated findings and work
Condenser obstruction is a technician visual estimate to the nearest five percentage points. It is not a whole-vehicle condition
score. Previous attention references may precede this selected extract. Full definitions and initial reference details are in the
monthly-history CSV handout.

sources.title: Daily usage
caveats: Fictional exercise data. Selected records are not full-fleet totals.
Recorded daily vehicle use
All timestamps Singapore UTC+08. Operating cohort: 5–16 October 2026; evidence cut-off 16 October 16:00. Blanks mean not supplied or
not applicable. Eight selected vehicles; all ten supplied weekdays.
Daily usage
Derived exactly from trips actual_vehicle_id and terminal_movements vehicle_id. In-service duration is departure to terminal
arrival; positioning duration uses actual_start/end. It excludes boarding before origin departure, final alighting, idle time and
unlisted duties. Integer seconds are authoritative; hours are rounded to six decimal places. Route distance and positioning distance
remain exercise source measurements. Exercise odometer equals the fictional 5 October baseline plus only supplied in-service route
distance and listed terminal-positioning distance. It is a reproducible exercise counter, not a claim of complete real odometer
readings: depot travel, other duties and unlisted movement are not measured or invented.

sources.title: Monthly use and odometers
caveats: Fictional exercise data. Selected records are not full-fleet totals.
Monthly vehicle use for eight buses
Fictional exercise records for eight selected buses, not all 172 fleet vehicles. Complete months: October 2024–September 2026. Zero
means none recorded in the monthly ledger. Vehicle ID and month identify the same record across the cost, maintenance and usage
views. Distance includes positioning. Running hours exclude stationary waiting, workshop time and crew breaks. No historical route

Monthly use and odometers

different coverage. September odometers precede the existing October baseline; the data dictionary explains the intervening
distance. Do not count repeated views as extra mileage.

# Monthly fleet history: coverage and definitions

All records are fictional LionLink exercise data. The files cover **eight selected buses**, not the complete 172-vehicle operating fleet. Currency is SGD excluding tax. Dates use Singapore local time.

The monthly history covers **1 October 2024 to 30 September 2026**. It contains one complete monthly summary for each of these eight vehicles: 192 rows. The financial comparison contains the same repair totals grouped into two equal twelve-month periods. It is a summary of the monthly file, not additional spending.

The earlier period is supplied as monthly summaries and twelve selected component observations. October 2026 remains available through the existing, more detailed job and operating extracts. This is a difference in the extracts supplied for the exercise; it does not imply that LionLink changed its recording systems.

## Repair spending by vehicle

`repair_spend_by_vehicle.csv` has sixteen rows. Its key is `period_start`, `period_end`, `vehicle_id`.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `period_start`, `period_end` | Inclusive dates of each complete twelve-month period: October–September. These are not calendar-year totals. |
| `vehicle_id` | Bus identifier shared with Engineering and Operations. |
| `repair_count` | Completed corrective repair jobs in the period; the sum of monthly repair counts. |
| `repair_cost_sgd` | Recorded parts and labour charges for those jobs; the sum of monthly repair charges. Scheduled services, additional preventive work and proposed quotes are excluded. |

## Monthly vehicle history

`monthly_vehicle_history.csv` has 192 rows. Its key is `month`, `vehicle_id`. Numeric fields are complete for the supplied monthly ledger: **zero means none recorded in that month**, not missing data. There are no missing monthly numeric values.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `month` | Calendar month in `YYYY-MM` form. |
| `vehicle_id` | Shared vehicle identifier. Vehicle type, capacity and in-service year remain in the existing vehicle register. |
| `recorded_km` | Total running distance in this monthly ledger, including positioning. It is a matched-period measure of use. It does not identify individual routes, trips or route difficulty. |
| `recorded_operating_hours` | Time running, including positioning; excludes stationary waiting, workshop time and crew breaks. |
| `month_end_exercise_odometer_km` | Fictional exercise odometer after the month's recorded movement. Consecutive month-end differences equal the later month's `recorded_km`. The first month's opening reading can be obtained by subtraction. |
| `repair_count` | Completed corrective repair jobs. A repair can follow a fault found between duties; this is **not a count of roadside breakdowns or cancelled trips**. Separate visits are separate jobs even when symptoms sound similar. |
| `repair_cost_sgd` | Incurred parts and labour charges for those repairs. Quotes and other maintenance categories are excluded. |
| `scheduled_service_count` | Completed required routine services. The supplied fictional requirements remain 600 recorded km or 14 calendar days, whichever comes first. |
| `scheduled_service_cost_sgd` | Charges for the routine services, including their ordinary visual checks. |
| `additional_preventive_visits` | Planned component checks or cleaning outside the required routine-service scope. These visits may concern different components. A count alone does not identify the work or its effectiveness. |
| `additional_preventive_cost_sgd` | Charges for that additional work; excluded from routine-service and repair charges. |
| `repair_unavailable_hours` | Elapsed time the vehicle was unavailable under corrective repair holds. Includes checks before release. It is not passenger delay or lost service time. |
| `scheduled_maintenance_unavailable_hours` | Elapsed vehicle unavailability for required routine service and additional preventive work, excluding any time already counted as a repair hold. |

The two unavailable-hour fields do not overlap in these monthly records. Add them to obtain the recorded maintenance unavailability. They do not show whether cover ran, which departures were affected or whether passengers waited longer. The monthly file contains no historical route assignments, complaint totals, cancellations or driver records.

## Selected component observations

`selected_component_observations.csv` has twelve selected visits, not the complete repair or inspection ledger. Its key is `observation_id`. Absence of a visit from this selected extract does not mean no other work happened.

| Fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `observation_id`, `observed_on`, `vehicle_id`, `component` | Visit reference, date, vehicle and component examined. |
| `exercise_odometer_km` | Fictional reading at the recorded check, consistent with the monthly totals. |
| `previous_component_attention_on`, `previous_component_attention_odometer_km` | Date and reading recorded for the previous cleaning or corrective attention to this component. Routine visual checks may take place in between; they do not reset this measure. These references can precede the selected visit extract. |
| `previous_observation_id` | Earlier visit in this extract, where included. Blank means that previous visit is referenced but not supplied as a separate observation row. |
| `km_since_component_attention` | Current reading minus the previous component-attention reading. It is not distance since the last required routine service. |
| `condenser_obstruction_before_pct`, `condenser_obstruction_after_pct` | Technician's visual estimate of the condenser face obstructed by debris, to the nearest five percentage points, before and after the recorded work. Blank means not applicable to the door component. This is not a general vehicle condition score. |
| `observed_condition`, `action_taken` | Workshop finding and recorded action. Different findings can occur when a vehicle returns with a similar symptom. |
| `work_category` | `repair` or `additional_preventive`; identifies the corresponding monthly cost/count category. |
| `charge_sgd`, `unavailable_hours` | Included parts/labour charge and vehicle hold for this visit. Both are already included in the corresponding monthly figures; do not add them again. |

For the initial prior-attention references, NW-V020's 5 December 2025 condenser clean, NW-V009's 13 January 2026 condenser clean and NW-V002's 12 December 2025 condenser clean were additional preventive visits. NW-V005's 10 December 2025 door-runner cleaning was included in its required routine service. Subsequent referenced actions can be followed directly through `previous_observation_id`. Additional preventive visits to other components do not reset a component's attention interval.

## Connecting to the existing detailed records

- Join by vehicle and the matching month or dates. Use the existing October Operations assignments when matching the October passenger cases. An October assigned service is not evidence of a bus's route throughout the preceding two years.
- September's monthly repair totals already include the **SGD450** NW-V020 hose repair on 28 September and the **SGD55** NW-V039 lighting repair on 30 September. These existing detailed jobs are included subsets, not extra charges.
- September month-end odometers precede the existing 4 October baseline service. The differences represent 1–4 October distance, outside this monthly table: NW-V001 60 km; NW-V002 40 km; NW-V005 80 km; NW-V009 100 km; NW-V020 50 km; NW-V039 60 km; NW-V050 30 km; NW-V140 20 km. Do not add these differences to September totals or to the 5–16 October usage extract.
- The October usage extract covers ten supplied weekday mornings and their downstream journeys, not a complete month. Do not compare its raw totals with complete-month totals, or divide two years of repairs by October-only mileage.
- The existing October Engineering extract is selected history. Its missing rows cannot be interpreted as zero repairs for a whole October month. Its jobs and service costs are outside the two complete twelve-month periods above.
- Historical summaries do not replace Engineering's current release decision. They do not establish a mechanical cause for October delays, driver-cover decisions, boarding queues or the separate evening incident.

The vehicle sample is small and selected. Comparisons can identify questions and proposed changes to test; they do not establish a whole-company cost forecast or a measured saving from an intervention.

# LionLink operating records

This exercise contains **real Singapore network geography and entirely fictional operating records**. Service numbers, ordered bus stops, bus stop coordinates and rail station relationships come from the attributed public network snapshot. All LionLink timetables, vehicles, drivers, passenger counts, control messages and service outcomes are synthetic. They do not describe SBS Transit, SMRT or any other real operator's performance.

The sample covers 24 bus services and their 36 published directional or loop patterns, retaining all 1,353 route-stop occurrences across 809 physical stops. There are ten fictional weekdays from 5 to 16 October 2026. Timetabled departures begin between 06:00 and 11:59; the records retain each journey's complete downstream calls, including arrivals after noon. This is a bounded morning cohort, not the whole bus system or a complete service day. Every date supplied is available for analysis; none is a hidden evaluation set.

Run `python3 scripts/rebuild_database.py` from the package root to create the optional `lionlink-network.sqlite`. It contains the same nineteen core tables as the CSVs in this directory, with numeric columns and useful indexes. The separate `workshop/` supplement adds eight held workshop vehicles for the operating console; it is not included in the core database and does not add dispatchable buses to the 172-vehicle timetable. Read `DATA_DICTIONARY.md` for keys, units and observation limits. Stop codes are text: retain leading zeroes. `route_id` identifies a direction or loop, while `service_no` identifies the passenger-facing service. `stop_order` is the dense visit order; `source_stop_sequence` preserves the original source values, including gaps.

Passenger records describe intended service-direction and route-position cohorts. They do not represent every person waiting at a shared stop. A repeated physical stop on a loop has separate cohorts for separate portions of the journey. Origin observations provide exact five-minute arrival batches for exercise replay; other stops provide counts between observed calls. Use each queue window's start/end and remaining queue rather than assuming all passengers boarded. The counting model groups boarding at a documented cutoff; it is not a second-by-second door simulation.

Timetables and resource windows are exercise assumptions. A proposed operational change must respect the supplied planning constraints, vehicle capacity, terminal movements, crew availability and later assignments. Issued timestamps distinguish what a controller knew at a decision from what later observations revealed. No unlisted spare resource, unseen earlier journey or unspecified later commitment should be invented.

Rail data provides real station membership and adjacency as geographical context. Connecting station points with a straight line does not describe track alignment, train running time or an accessible walking transfer. The sample contains no observed train operations or passenger transfer outcomes. Geographical proximity alone is not evidence that two journeys are interchangeable.

These operating records are the shared fleet and service history for the Engineering and Customer Service handouts. Their selected vehicle records use these same `NW-V` identifiers and their passenger reports concern journeys within 5–16 October 2026. Request those handouts from IT / Data when needed. They are supplied separately and are not additional tables in this database. A selected maintenance history is not complete history for every vehicle, and a passenger account is not an independently verified explanation of a service event.

The rail-relief, maintenance-planning and festival handouts extend this same fleet into explicitly dated evening or future duties. Their own issued records supply the relevant commitments, locations and release conditions. Morning availability alone does not establish availability for those later duties.

# Data dictionary

All operating records are fictional. Public network fields retain their source identifiers. CSV and SQLite table names match. Timestamps use ISO 8601 with `+08:00`; durations are seconds unless a column explicitly says minutes. Counts are people, distances are kilometres and coordinates are WGS84 decimal degrees. Empty text means not supplied, not zero.

The table below describes the nineteen core CSV/SQLite tables. The separate `workshop/` register supplement is documented at the end and is not inside the core SQLite database.

| Table | Grain / key | Meaning and joins |
|---|---|---|
| `routes` | `route_id` | One source direction or loop. `service_no`, `direction`, `service_name`, `operator`, origin/destination stop IDs, stop count, source route distance, loop flag and source ID. Operator attribution belongs to the network, not the synthetic performance. |
| `stops` | `stop_id` | Public five-character bus stop code, description, road name, latitude, longitude and source ID. |
| `route_stops` | `route_id`, `stop_order` | Complete source stop sequence. `source_stop_sequence` retains published gaps. `distance_km` is cumulative source distance, not straight-line distance. First/last service strings are source HHMM values, not a full timetable; after-midnight values may exceed 2400. |
| `rail_stations` | `station_id` | Public station name and grouped station/line codes (`|` separated), coordinates, coordinate derivation and snapshot date. Interchange station IDs can combine multiple codes. |
| `rail_links` | `edge_id` | Public adjacent station pairs with line code/name and source URL. `bidirectional_topology` concerns adjacency only; schematic geometry is not track distance or a train timetable. |
| `service_calendar` | `service_date` | Supplied fictional dates, day type and timezone. |
| `service_patterns` | `route_id` | Synthetic published headway assumptions, departure window, peak interval, running allowance and terminal minimum. `morning_first_departure` and period bounds are local clock times. A trip already scheduled before a period boundary keeps its previous headway to the next departure. The `trips` table is authoritative for the resulting timetable. |
| `vehicles` | `vehicle_id` | Fictional vehicle, assigned service, SD/DD type, usable total-person capacity and wheelchair spaces. These capacities are exercise assumptions. |
| `crew_duties` | `duty_id`; unique date/crew | Fictional qualifications (one service), availability, start location, protected break, takeover requirement, maximum continuous duty and record issue time. Duty includes vehicle tasks; breaks contain no tasks. IDs may repeat on different dates. |
| `vehicle_readiness` | `readiness_id`; date/vehicle | Issued release state, availability, initial location and usable capacity. Subsequent commitments are in trips and movements. |
| `trips` | `trip_id` | Published and observed departure/terminal-arrival times, planned block/vehicle/crew, actual vehicle/crew, route, service and terminal IDs. Arrival is before final terminal alighting. `completion_state` describes this supplied trip. `published_distance_km` is source route distance. |
| `stop_calls` | `call_id`; trip/stop order | Complete visit chronology and passenger ledger. Every trip visits every source occurrence, including the final terminal. See accounting definitions below. |
| `queue_windows` | `queue_window_id`; date/route/stop order | Exact scope of each intended route-position cohort, initial queue, arrivals, boardings and final remaining queue. Observation ends at the last supplied call; later arrivals are outside this total. |
| `origin_arrivals` | `arrival_record_id` | Synthetic five-minute arrival batches at each route origin. All people in a row are assigned that row's timestamp for a reproducible coarse replay. Use only events within a queue window when reconciling totals. Extra arrivals after the last observed trip do not belong to that window. |
| `terminal_movements` | `movement_id` | Actual non-service positioning between trips when terminal stop codes differ, with bus, driver, endpoints and times. Distance/time are explicitly synthetic planning allowances, not verified road journeys. There is no invented reverse passenger direction. |
| `resource_updates` | `update_id` | Contemporaneous resource reports: `issued_at`, location, effective availability and related trip. `resource_id` may combine vehicle and crew with `|`. |
| `control_actions` | `action_id` | Recorded dispatch instructions with issue time, trip, selected resources and referenced update IDs (`|` separated). Notes are operator statements within the fiction, not validated diagnoses. |
| `planning_constraints` | `constraint_id` | Exercise requirements for proposals and retrospective comparisons. |
| `timetable_records` | `version_id` | Issue time and effective dates of the synthetic timetable. |

## Stop-call accounting

`scheduled_arrival_at` is the published arrival at the stop occurrence. At the origin it includes a 120-second boarding window before published departure. `actual_arrival_at` and `actual_departure_at` delimit the observed stop dwell; `boarding_cutoff_at` is the counting cutoff: departure minus five seconds at origins, doors opening at intermediate stops. Boarding takes 1.2 seconds per person plus five seconds clearance. Origin batches board FIFO; a person can only start boarding after their arrival and the previous person finishes. Intermediate counts conservatively admit only the cohort present when doors open; people arriving during dwell enter the next observation interval. This is a deliberate aggregate-count approximation, not a door-level pedestrian simulation. Final terminals allow 45 seconds alighting and have no boarding for that completed trip.

`onboard_arriving` is before alighting. `alighted_people` leave the vehicle; `boarded_people` then enter. `onboard_departing = onboard_arriving - alighted_people + boarded_people`, within `capacity_people`. Every trip starts empty and passengers remaining onboard alight at its final terminal. A passenger's individual destination is not provided; do not invent an OD matrix from aggregate alightings.

`arrivals_since_previous_call` counts new arrivals in the route-position cohort since its previous cutoff, or since the window start for its first call. `queue_before_people` includes the previous remaining queue plus these new arrivals. `queue_after_people = queue_before_people - boarded_people`. Remaining passengers carry forward to the next observed call for this cohort; they are not counted again as new arrivals. No abandonment or route switching is modelled. Within a window, `initial_queue_people + total_arrivals_people = total_boarded_people + remaining_queue_people`.

For the queue ledger, order calls by `boarding_cutoff_at`, then `trip_id`, then `stop_order` to break exact ties. CSV row order groups a trip's visits for convenience. Two buses can dwell at the same stop at once: the earlier doors-opening cutoff reserves its observed cohort first even if that bus departs second. Do not reorder that queue ledger by departure time.

Ordinary stop counts support occupancy, boarding, queue and service-regularity analysis. Exact individual waiting times outside the origin arrival batches are unavailable. Do not use window boundaries as proof that there was no earlier/later demand. Shared-stop totals may be summed only with their distinct cohort definitions intact, and must not be read as unique cross-service travellers.

## Resource timing

After terminal arrival, final alighting takes 45 seconds and minimum vehicle turnaround takes 420 seconds before the next departure, including the 120-second origin boarding window. Turnaround is not a driver rest break. Different terminal codes may require a listed movement; those movements follow turnaround, then a further 120-second boarding window is required. A five-minute driver takeover may overlap stationary turnaround. The driver doing a listed terminal movement is explicitly recorded and may differ from the next passenger trip's driver.

The continuous duty limit and protected breaks are fictional exercise rules. Availability windows are sufficient for the listed actual tasks; other periods of a driver's day are outside scope. Retrospective comparisons must retain later commitments and distinguish publication/issue time from effective time and eventual observation.

## Related Engineering and passenger handouts

The separately supplied Engineering and Customer Service workbooks use the same operating vehicle identifiers and service dates as these tables. They are not extra tables in this SQLite database. Engineering contains selected histories for eight operating vehicles, with dated earlier lookback and work after supplied morning duties. Its `vehicle_id` matches `vehicles.vehicle_id`; work orders, services and inspections retain their own record identifiers.

Passenger reports contain a `journey_window_start`, `journey_window_end` and `journey_time_basis`, plus available `reported_service_no`, `reported_vehicle_id` and `reported_stop_id`. The time basis distinguishes an expected departure from an observed departure. Service numbers match `trips.service_no`; reported fleet numbers refer to a vehicle, not a route number. Match the supplied date, window and identifiers to the relevant trip and stop record before treating a relationship as established. Preserve the distinction between planned and actual vehicles.

The evening incident and future planning handouts use this same fleet with explicit additional duty and release records. Read their issue times and coverage; an available morning vehicle is not automatically available later. Passenger accounts, mechanical findings and operating chronology provide different kinds of evidence and do not establish a shared cause by themselves.

## Workshop-only register supplement

The `workshop/` directory adds two separate CSVs for a fictional held-only cohort. NW-W001 through NW-W008 do not belong to the 172 operating vehicles in the core tables and have no supplied trips or release records. The console may show 180 register entries, but only 172 belong to the operating cohort. Missing work orders never prove that a vehicle is released.

`workshop_vehicles.csv` has one row per additional vehicle: `vehicle_id`, `vehicle_type`, `capacity_people`, `wheelchair_spaces`, `fleet_scope`, `facility_id` and `record_issued_at`. NW-WS01 is the fictional North Workshop and NW-WS02 the fictional Central Workshop; no real depot location is asserted.

`workshop_work_orders.csv` has one row per work order: `work_order_id`, `vehicle_id`, `opened_at`, `updated_at`, `facility_id`, `fault_summary`, `work_status`, `expected_completion_at`, `confirmed_release_at`, `release_status` and `workshop_note`. The record is known only after its issue/update timestamp. Every supplied release status is `held`, and every confirmed release field is empty. An estimated completion remains an estimate when its timestamp passes; do not invent a later release or work-stage update.

The collections below describe different populations and kinds of evidence.
Their totals are not interchangeable.

| Source                                  | Coverage                                                                                                     | What it supports                                                                           |

| Monthly vehicle history                 | Eight selected vehicles, October 2024–September 2026.                                                        | Comparisons of recorded costs, distance, and vehicle unavailability.                       |
| Repair summaries and work orders        | Annual summaries and selected maintenance visits.                                                            | Detail about repair activity; coverage can overlap the monthly history.                    |
| Operating journey and stop-call records | Departures scheduled from 06:00 to 11:59 on ten weekdays, 5–16 October 2026, with downstream calls retained. | Departure timing, arrival delay, boarding activity, and recorded queues within that scope. |
| Passenger accounts                      | Six selected accounts received by phone or through the web.                                                  | Descriptions of particular experiences and identifiers for possible journey matches.       |
| Workshop planning records               | Proposed requests, resource capacity, and service-cover constraints.                                         | Assessment of whether proposed work fits the available resources.                          |
| Cost proposals                          | Quoted packages with specified work, exclusions, and validity periods.                                       | Comparison of proposed prices and scope; not actual spending or measured savings.          |

## Evidence limits

All business records are fictional exercise data. Dates and times use Singapore
local time. Costs are SGD excluding tax.

The maintenance sample does not represent every operating vehicle. The operating
extract is not a continuous, all-day service history. Selected passenger accounts
do not establish a network complaint rate.

A plan is not a completed job, and a quote is not an approved purchase. These
records alone do not establish causal effects, customer retention, or guaranteed savings.

Use this procedure when you need to decide whether a measure changed between two
periods. Start with the records and coverage notes for both periods.

1. **Define the question.** Specify the measure you want to compare. Total repair
   spending and repair cost per kilometre answer different questions.
2. **Match the population.** Use the same vehicles or services in both periods.
   If membership changed, report that difference alongside the result.
3. **Match the time coverage.** Compare complete periods of equal length. For
   operating records, check the days of the week and scheduled departure windows.
4. **Use the same definition and unit.** Check which costs or events are included.
   Keep quoted prices separate from incurred spending and plans separate from outcomes.
5. **Account for activity.** Compare repair charges with recorded kilometres, for
   example. Use a denominator from the same population and period as the numerator.
6. **State the result with its scope.** Include the population, periods, unit, and
   source. Describe gaps that limit the comparison.

Do not add totals with overlapping coverage. Monthly records and an annual summary
may describe the same spending. If the available records cannot support a matched
comparison, describe the periods separately.

See [Measures and coverage](/docs/measures/) for definitions and
[the maintenance comparison](/docs/maintenance-findings/) for an example.

ranking of value or a recommendation to buy.

## Compare scope before price

The chart shows each quoted package in full. A package with four visits cannot
be read as a single-visit price, and a diagnostic review does not include every
repair it might identify.



The option identifiers refer to these scopes:

- **NW-OPT001** is a targeted HVAC review. Parts and corrective work are quoted separately.
- **NW-OPT002** is four planned cleaning and checking visits. Some cleaning overlaps routine service.
- **NW-OPT003** is a fan assembly replacement, conditional on Engineering establishing that replacement is justified.
- **NW-OPT005** is an inspection of a comparison vehicle. It is not a requirement to repair a healthy vehicle.

Overlapping work must not be added as if every option were a separate necessary
purchase. The records provide no measured savings or guaranteed reduction in faults.

## Keep the replacement proposal separate

The fleet replacement option is a capital proposal with a different scope and
lead time. It excludes finance, infrastructure, resale, and transition costs.
Putting it beside a maintenance visit as though the two solve the same problem
would omit those differences.

Historical repair spending provides context; it does not prove
that a proposed replacement or preventive package is economical.

Use this procedure to check whether the available records support a finding.
Start with the claim and its source citation.

1. **Identify the source.** Note the collection, reporting period, and population.
   [Evidence sources](/docs/applications/) describes the supplied collections.
2. **Identify the relevant records.** Match vehicle identifiers for maintenance
   questions. For journey questions, match service, date, stop, and journey time.
3. **Distinguish scheduled and observed values.** A scheduled departure describes
   the plan; an actual departure describes the recorded event. Do not substitute
   one for the other when matching a passenger account to a journey.
4. **Check the calculation.** Confirm that each included record belongs to the
   stated scope. Check the unit and denominator against
   [Measures and coverage](/docs/measures/).
5. **Check for overlap and gaps.** Do not count an annual summary again alongside
   its monthly records. Do not treat a missing value as zero without source evidence.
6. **Record what remains unresolved.** Cite the records that support the finding
   and identify any missing evidence needed to answer the question.

A matching record can locate an event without explaining its cause. Keep the
observed result separate from any proposed explanation.

sources.text:
In this exercise, you will compare repair spending across two years, account for
recorded distance, and write a conclusion supported by both measures.

Use the two graphs and their source tables in
[Why repair spending needs a distance comparison](/docs/maintenance-findings/).

## Establish the scope

Read the source caption beneath the first graph. Both years cover the same eight
selected buses, and each year runs from October to September.

Write down that scope before comparing the values. Your conclusion will concern
those buses over those years, rather than the whole operating fleet.

## Compare the repair charges

In the first graph's source table, compare the repair charges for the two years.
The later year has higher charges. Routine servicing and additional preventive
work are separate categories; leave them out of a comparison of repairs alone.

At this point, you can conclude that recorded repair spending increased. You
cannot yet tell whether the increase simply reflects more distance travelled.

## Account for distance

Read the recorded kilometres, then compare the rates in the second graph.
Each rate divides repair charges by kilometres for the same year and multiplies
the result by 1,000.

Both distance and repair charges increased, but repair charges grew faster.
The higher rate means the selected buses incurred more repair cost per recorded
kilometre in the later year.

## Write the conclusion

A conclusion supported by these records is:

> For the eight selected buses, repair spending increased between the two complete
> October–September years. Repair cost per 1,000 km also increased, so the rise in
> recorded distance alone does not account for the rise in spending.

The comparison does not identify the cause. Vehicle condition and individual
repair records would be needed to investigate why costs changed.

You have now distinguished a total, a rate, and a causal explanation. For another
comparison, follow [Compare report periods](/docs/compare-reports/).

sources.text:
## Maintenance measures

The historical reports use these measures:

| Measure                   | Meaning                                                                                              |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Recorded maintenance cost | Repair charges plus routine service and additional preventive work.                                  |
| Repair cost per 1,000 km  | Repair charges divided by kilometres recorded for the same vehicles and period, multiplied by 1,000. |
| Corrective repairs        | Recorded repair jobs, not the number of vehicles repaired.                                           |
| Vehicle unavailability    | Vehicle hold hours recorded for repairs or scheduled maintenance. Not passenger delay time.          |

The history covers eight selected vehicles from October 2024 to September 2026.
Monthly records, annual summaries, and selected work orders can overlap.
All monetary figures are SGD excluding tax.

## Operating measures

The operating reports use these measures:

| Measure                               | Meaning                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Early departure                       | Departure before its scheduled time.                                                                                  |
| Departure within the five-minute band | Departure from zero to five minutes after its scheduled time, inclusive.                                              |
| Late departure                        | Departure more than five minutes after its scheduled time.                                                            |
| Mean arrival delay                    | Average recorded arrival delay, in minutes.                                                                           |
| 90th-percentile arrival delay         | The value at the 90th percentile of recorded delays. It shows the slower end of the distribution, not the worst trip. |
| Boardings                             | Boarding events. A person who boards more than once can appear more than once.                                        |
| Calls with a remaining queue          | Stop calls at which people remain waiting after boarding.                                                             |
| Departures at capacity                | Stop calls where the departing onboard count equals the recorded capacity.                                            |

The extract covers scheduled departures from 06:00 to 11:59 on ten weekdays,
5–16 October 2026. Complete downstream calls for those journeys are retained.
It is not an all-day or continuous service record. Dates and times are Singapore
local time.

## Planning and cost options

Workshop requests and proposed allocations are plans. Tentative completion times
are not confirmed Engineering releases. A quoted price is not incurred spending
or an approved purchase.

## Evidence limits

The supplied records are fictional exercise data.

The current reports do not establish that an intervention caused a change,
increased customer retention, or will produce a guaranteed saving.

sources.text:
The supplied records contain six selected passenger accounts received by phone
or through the web. They describe particular experiences. They are not a complete
survey of passengers or a representative measure of service quality.

## The channel counts describe this selection

More of these selected accounts came through the web than by phone. That does not
establish which channel all passengers prefer or which produces more complaints
relative to the number of people using it.



## A journey match identifies an event, not its cause

Stop details, journey windows, and supplied identifiers help identify a possible
match between a passenger account and an operating journey. Expected
journeys use scheduled departure times; observed journeys use actual departures.

A matched trip helps locate the event. It does not establish why an experience
occurred or confirm every detail of the account. A comfort report, for example,
needs condition and maintenance evidence before it can support a diagnosis.

## Boardings are not customer retention

Repeated boarding observations can show activity on recorded dates. They do not
identify which people returned, why someone stopped travelling, or whether a
service change caused growth.

These accounts provide evidence of reported experiences. Without a representative
sample or a passenger denominator, they cannot establish how common those
experiences are.

The five-minute band is a counting rule. It does not mean every journey

after leaving its origin.

The mean recorded arrival delay is **[value in original report] minutes**.
The 90th percentile is **[value in original report] minutes**.

A service-level or day-level average can still conceal a particular late journey.

Only departures scheduled from 06:00 to 11:59 are included. Their full downstream
journeys are retained, but this is not evidence for every evening or weekend trip.
The extract covers ten weekdays in October 2026 and cannot establish a long-term trend.

The graph shows requested resources, not resources consumed by completed work.
It does not establish which plan was chosen, whether either job finished, or what
service disruption occurred. The same distinction applies to festival proposals
and incident assumptions in the supplied planning records.
